useful_material: This study reports a re-analysis of plasma metabolomic data from renal cell carcinoma (RCC) patients in the CheckMate 025 trial (nivolumab vs everolimus), finding that higher baseline plasma inosine levels correlate with longer overall survival specifically in the nivolumab arm (median OS 33 months vs 22 months for high vs low groups). The authors confirm that metabolic profiling of ICB-treated human cancers supports the association between inosine levels and ICB sensitivity. Mechanistically, the study identifies that inosine directly inhibits the ubiquitin-activating enzyme UBA6 in tumor cells, enhancing tumor immunogenicity and MHC-I expression, rather than acting primarily on T cells. This provides a specific molecular link between a microbiota-associated metabolite (inosine) and tumor-intrinsic resistance to ICB.

useful_material: This prospective study enrolled 39 patients with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (mNSCLC) treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) alone or with chemotherapy. The authors collected fecal and tumor samples prior to ICI initiation. Fecal short-chain fatty acids (SCFA) were measured by LC-MS/MS, and tumoral transcriptome profiling was performed via RNA sequencing. The study reported that high levels of fecal propionate correlated with significantly longer overall survival (p=0.02) and were increased in the high fiber diet group compared to the low fiber group. At the tumor level, RNA sequencing demonstrated upregulation of humoral and adaptive immune responses in the high fiber group. However, the text specifies fecal SCFA measurement and tumor transcriptomics; it does not explicitly report absolute concentrations of SCFAs or inosine within the tumor tissue itself.
